newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Croats evict Moslems after violence in Mostar.
newsitem.headline: Croats evict Moslems after violence in Mostar.

text.p: Bosnian Croats stepped up their evictions of Moslems in the divided city of Mostar on Monday, hours after the worst ethnic violence since the war ended in 1995 claimed at least one dead and 22 wounded Moslems.
"There were at least 8 expulsions in one hour tonight. Croats were expelling all Moslems from one building," the officer of the NATO-led Stabilisation Force (SFOR) in Mostar told Reuters.

Evictions of Moslems from the western Croat-controlled part of the city have become a regular occurrence, and Western officials have blamed them on local mafia gangs, approved or at least condoned by the Croat authorities.

SFOR troops, which have no power of arrest, arrived at the scene, while U.N. International Police were confined to their police stations because of the rising violence in the town, another NATO official said.

The violence occurred in the early afternoon, when 500 Moslems headed to the Liska cemetery on the Croat side of the city and some 700 Croats in a Roman Catholic carnival parade tried to block them, said SFOR spokesman Major Tony White.
Monday was the second day of the Islamic religious holiday of Bairam, when Moslems mourn their dead.
Alija Behram, a radio journalist from the Moslem-controlled eastern sector, said the mob began beating some of the Moslems and then shots rang out, spreading panic among the crowd.

NATO sources said shots were believed to have been fired at the Moslems during the street confrontation. "There were 22 injured, two seriously, and one dead," White said, adding all casualties were Moslem.
Mike Fabbro, SFOR spokesman in Mostar, told Reuters there were "photographs which confirmed eyewitness accounts that Croats, including policemen, had opened fire on the crowd."
A dusk-to-dawn curfew on both sides of the divided town was promptly ordered by Valentin Coric, a Croat who is the Interior Minister for Hercegovina-Neretva canton, which includes Mostar.
Shortly after the violence, the bloodiest in Mostar since NATO troops deployed in Bosnia in late 1995, groups of militant Croats and Moslems gathered on each side of the former confrontation line.
SFOR deployed some 100 Spanish troops to the town centre to defuse the tension and the crowd dispersed towards the evening.
The Moslem-controlled Bosnian state radio accused Croat policemen of firing on the pilgrims while nationalist Croat media accused Moslems of provoking tension.
The Croatian state news agency HINA said 18 Croat policemen were injured, but this could not be independently confirmed.
However, Pierre Bayle, chief SFOR spokesman in Mostar, told Reuters two Croat truck drivers were beaten up by Moslems on the outskirts of the town in the evening.
The night was quiet but Fabbro said an explosion was reported at about 2000 GMT, adding it was not clear on which side of town it took place.
Carl Bildt, the international High Representative to postwar Bosnia, issued a statement expressing outrage at what he called a murderous attack.
"We condemn in the strongest possible terms the indiscriminate killing of innocent civilians in Mostar today. This is murder, and must be treated as such," Bildt said in the statement from Sarajevo.

Bildt's deputy Michael Steiner held urgent meetings with local government officials in Mostar on Monday evening. "If it turns out some officials were involved in the incident they must bear legal consequences," he told reporters.
Croat Kresimir Zubak, president of the Moslem-Croat Federation called for an "objective" investigation into the incident by mixed Moslem-Croat police.
"We're sure there is a small group of extremists who are responsible for this," Fabbro said.
